analysis.one_liner: Lets states take over oil and gas permitting on federal land, exempt from federal environmental laws.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: referred to the House Natural Resources Committee in February 2015, it got one subcommittee hearing in November 2015 and no vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let any state with its own oil and gas rules declare federal land inside its borders open for drilling under state permits instead of federal ones. Once a state made that declaration, its actions would no longer count as federal actions, so they would be exempt from the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act. Oil and gas companies could get drilling permits from state regulators faster and without federal environmental reviews, endangered species consultations, or federal court challenges.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that want to drill on the roughly 113 million acres of federal land the bill described as open and accessible [S3]. They would get permits from state regulators, which the bill's sponsors said took far less time than the 197-day federal average [S3], and the permits could not be challenged or delayed under the main federal environmental laws [S3]. State governments would gain authority over drilling on federal land within their borders and could keep permit application fees [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas drillers on federal land

how_it_helps.text: A state with an established leasing, permitting, and regulatory program could declare that program to the Secretaries of Interior, Agriculture, and Energy and take over responsibility for leasing, permitting, and regulating oil and gas development on federal land in the state [S2] [S3].

State-issued leases and permits would not be subject to the Administrative Procedure Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, the Endangered Species Act, or the National Environmental Policy Act, removing federal environmental review, species consultations, and judicial review from the process [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings cite delays as the problem: 197 days to process federal drilling permits in 2013, federal land leased for oil and gas down 24 percent since 2008, and about 166 million acres described as off-limits or inaccessible [S3].

Royalties and other revenues would still be collected at the same amounts and deposited in the same federal Treasury accounts as if the federal government had issued the lease, so federal revenue would not change [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the environmental and public-input costs. Federal land is managed on behalf of all Americans, but the bill would remove the National Environmental Policy Act review that gives communities notice and a chance to comment before drilling begins, and the Endangered Species Act consultation that protects wildlife. Anyone harmed by a state permit would also lose the ability to challenge the decision in federal court under the Administrative Procedure Act [S3]. The bill excludes national parks, wildlife refuges, and designated wilderness, but not other sensitive federal land [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near federal land and the public

drawbacks.text: Removing National Environmental Policy Act review eliminates the standard process where the public gets notice of proposed drilling and a chance to comment before it starts; state-level permitting would replace that with whatever notice each state's own law provides [S3].

Exempting state actions from the Endangered Species Act and the National Historic Preservation Act would mean no federal consultation on threats to listed species or to historic and cultural sites on federal land, and the Administrative Procedure Act exemption would cut off federal court review of state permitting decisions [S3].

Federal land belongs to all Americans, but a single state's regulators would control drilling decisions on it, which raises the concern that the people most affected include citizens of other states who would have no say in that state's rules.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that state oil and gas programs vary widely in stringency, so the same drilling that would be carefully reviewed under federal rules in one state could face little scrutiny in another; the bill sets no minimum state standards beyond an established program [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver a real, targeted benefit: faster drilling permits for oil and gas companies, which its sponsors framed as jobs, energy production, and federal revenue. But the savings come almost entirely from cutting the public out of the process — no federal environmental review, no endangered species consultation, no historic preservation review, and no federal court challenge. The federal Treasury would keep the same royalties [S3], so the revenue argument does not change; what changes is who reviews and who can object. Weighing faster permits for an industry against removing the main legal protections governing drilling on land owned by all Americans, the costs fall more broadly than the benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee, which held a hearing but never advanced it, and the 114th Congress ended without a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 11, 2015, by Rep. Diane Black with 23 cosponsors, all Republicans [S1] [S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day, and to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources in March 2015 [S5].
The subcommittee held a hearing on November 15, 2015, but the full committee never marked up the bill and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who use or value federal land kept existing federal environmental review and court protections, because the bill died without a vote. Oil and gas operators on federal land continue to go through the longer federal permitting process the bill aimed to eliminate.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, none were Democrats, and the bill never reached a recorded vote.

industries.note: Drillers on federal land would get state permits that skip federal environmental review, endangered species consultation, and court challenges [S3]. Their gain comes at the cost of removing public notice and legal protections on land owned by all Americans [S3].

industries.industry: State governments and their oil and gas regulators
industries.note: States would take over leasing, permitting, and regulation of oil and gas on federal land within their borders and could keep application processing fees [S3]. The benefit to a state's residents is real, but the state would also be controlling land that belongs to citizens nationwide.

industries.industry: Federal land management agencies (Interior, Agriculture, Energy)
industries.note: The Departments would lose their authority to lease and permit oil and gas development on available federal land, along with the permitting revenues states could keep [S3].
